claims.claim: UST_mean reports Hyperliquid book-feed latency on Tokyo production: public WebSocket p50 236 ms, p90 346 ms, ~2% of frames over 1 s; Quicknode gRPC p50 176 ms, p90 211 ms, frames over 1 s 0.02%.

The tweet says the Quicknode Build plan costs $49/month with 80M credits, ~20 coins of best-bid/offer were enough, and a self-run validator would cost about $1,000/month; it also reports p90 cross-exchange slippage of 2-8 bp.

In June 2026 Hyperliquid's core team announced public WebSocket feeds would push less often: default l2Book 20 levels every 2 s, l2Book fast 5 levels every 0.5 s, allMids every 5 s, and advised automated traders to run a non-validating node.
Hyperliquid docs: l2Book is pushed on each block at least 0.5 since the last push; bbo is sent only if the best bid/offer changes on a block.
Hyperliquid public WebSocket limits: 10 connections, 1000 subscriptions, 2000 messages sent per minute; REST 1200 weight per minute per IP.
Hyperliquid docs state HyperBFT end-to-end latency for a co-located client is median 0.2 s and 99th percentile 0.9 s, and mainnet supports roughly 200k orders/sec.
Glassnode's March 2026 test placed 120 real market orders from AWS Tokyo and measured median order-to-fill of 884 ms (range 695-1634 ms), about 5 ms network and ~879 ms processing.

Quicknode's Hyperliquid gRPC API exposes StreamL2Book, StreamL4Book, StreamBboBook, StreamL2BookDiff, StreamL4BookUpdates and StreamTpslUpdates; order book methods are metered 10 credits per 0.0165 MB, StreamBboBook 10 credits per 0.00165 MB; Build plan or higher required.
Quicknode Build plan is $49/month ($42 annual) with 80M API credits, 50 requests/second and $0.62 per additional 1M credits.

The hyperliquid-dex/node README specifies non-validator 16 vCPU/128 GB RAM/500 GB SSD and validator 32 vCPU/128 GB/1 TB on Ubuntu 24.04, roughly 100 GB of logs per day by default, and recommends Tokyo for lowest latency.
An AWS r6i.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 128 GiB) costs $1.216 per hour on-demand in Tokyo ap-northeast-1 per third-party price aggregators.

Quicknode's March 2026 provider comparison lists Dwellir dedicated node at $1,150/month, Dwellir order-book server benchmark of 24.1% median improvement over the public feed across 2,662 trades, Hydromancer plans from $300 to $2,500/month, and notes order placement cannot go through any private provider.
Quicknode states Hyperliquid HyperCore produces blocks at about 12 blocks per second under normal conditions.
Hyperliquid perps base-tier (14-day volume under $5M) fees are 0.045% taker and 0.015% maker; top tier above $7B is 0.024% taker and 0%.
Hyperliquid funding settles hourly at one eighth of the 8-hour rate, premium sampled every 5 seconds, interest component 0.01% per 8 hours, capped at 4% per hour, paid on oracle price.

Aquilina, Budish and O'Neill estimate latency-arbitrage races are about one-third of price impact and effective spread, a ~0.5 bp tax, with modal race lasting 5-10 microseconds and six firms taking over 80% of wins and losses.

Budish, Cramton and Shim (QJE 2015) find correlations between ES and SPY break down at high-frequency horizons, that competition raised the speed bar rather than shrinking arbitrage, and propose frequent batch auctions roughly every tenth of a second.
Deribit's DVOL 30-day bitcoin implied volatility was 38.28 on 2026-10-20, while 14-day realized volatility was 20.2% and 30-day 28.9%.
Quicknode's StreamL2Book example output carries block_number, a millisecond time field, coin, and bids/asks arrays with px, sz and n; StreamL2Book delivers a full aggregated snapshot every block.
ARA scenario assumption: a StreamBboBook update is about 100 bytes on the wire; Quicknode docs publish the 0.00165 MB metering unit but not a per-message size.
Quicknode gRPC cut the median book-feed latency by about 25%.
assumptions: Tweet's before/after medians are comparable measurements
